abstract: |
  Video game research often treats games as a monolithic category, and single-game or single-platform studies leave open whether findings generalise across the medium. In this registered report, we used multi-platform digital trace data from the Open Play dataset to test whether (H1) total playtime is meaningfully associated with mental wellbeing and (H2) whether this association differs by game genre. The data comprise 226,000 hours of playtime telemetry across 4,154 titles from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam for 1,838 UK and US adults, linked to structured genre metadata and to 6,680 biweekly mental wellbeing assessments (SWEMWBS). Bayesian multilevel within-between models evaluated both hypotheses against a preregistered threshold for practical significance. Total playtime and genre-level playtime both showed the same pattern: associations with wellbeing were consistently under the threshold for practical significance. Wave-to-wave fluctuations in total playtime showed no meaningful link to wellbeing, and differences in habitual playtime across participants were similarly negligible. Contrary to our prediction, genre-level playtime did not meaningfully diverge from this pattern: genre heterogeneity was practically negligible under a hierarchical prior and inconclusive but small in the other specifications, including a multi-membership model for multi-genre games, with no evidence that any genre differed meaningfully from the rest. A daily-level exploratory analysis replicated this pattern. Genre differences appear to be the wrong place to look for gaming's wellbeing effects as genre labels are too coarse a proxy for the psychological experiences that plausibly drive them, which directs attention towards finer-grained characterisations of play.
categories: [video games, wellbeing, genres, digital trace data, registered report]

# Introduction

Video game effects research utilising digital trace data often focuses on a single game or a handful of games to understand the psychological processes and outcomes of digital play [@bruhlmannMotivationalProfilingLeague2020; @JohannesEtAl2021video; @larrieuHowGamingMotives2023; @ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025]. While understandable given the limited resources and lack of objective data available to independent researchers, it has left the field guessing whether identified relationships are unique to the studied titles or whether they apply universally across games.

Identifying how different types of games and gameplay affect wellbeing is vital in light of well-established evidence that playtime in general is not a meaningful predictor of wellbeing, using data from both specific games [@larrieuHowGamingMotives2023] and platforms [@ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024; @ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025]. This relationship, however, has not yet been tested using comprehensive multi-platform play data.

Multiple mechanisms have been proposed to explain why aggregate playtime is poorly predictive of wellbeing, including displacement of beneficial activities, satisfaction or frustration of basic psychological needs, and selection effects whereby individuals with lower wellbeing play more [@ballouHowVideoGames2025]. Most proposed mechanisms operate at the level of game features or player experience rather than at the level of total time spent; playtime is, at best, a moderator [@ballouHowVideoGames2025]. In causal terms, playing is a compound exposure that comes in many versions, so an average association across all of them answers an ambiguous question [@magnusson2024harmful]. The few causal analyses to date, exploiting console lotteries in Japan as natural experiments, found positive effects of console ownership on wellbeing that differed by console type and replicated in the post-pandemic period [@egami2024causal; @egamiCausalEffectVideo2026], suggesting that observational null findings may reflect confounding rather than absence of effect.

## Game Genres and Wellbeing

Consistent null findings for the effects of playtime on wellbeing have generated calls for the unpacking of raw decontextualised playtime into more informative measures that consider games' varied characteristics and affordances [@ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024]. Game genres offer a structured way to differentiate between video games and their corresponding play experiences [@starostaTangledWaysClassify2024]. Genre differences in player behaviour, cognition, and gaming disorder symptoms are well established [@andreRelationshipGameGenre2024; @dobrowolskiCognitiveEnhancementVideo2015; @raithMassivelyMultiplayerOnline2021; @hazelExploringPossibleMental2022]. Action games have been linked to increased visual attention [@palausNeuralBasisVideo2017], cognitive and attentional control [@angueraVideoGameTraining2013; @bavelierEnhancingAttentionalControl2019], and working memory [@blackerEffectsActionVideo2014]. Massively multiplayer online role-playing games (MMORPGs), first-person shooters, real-time strategy games (RTS), and Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) games have been associated with higher gaming disorder symptoms [@elliottContributionGameGenre2012; @naInfluenceGameGenre2017; @kingMaladaptivePlayergameRelationships2019; @rehbeinContributionGameGenre2021]. Player experience also differs by genre: MOBA players report less immersion and autonomy and more frustration than players of single-player genres [@johnsonAllThatBase2015a], and role-playing games are the genre players most often perceive as beneficial [@hazelExploringPossibleMental2022]. Randomised controlled trials with casual games and exergames induced positive moods and reduced stress [@huangImpactPlayingExergames2017; @russonielloEffectivenessCasualVideo2009]. These findings suggest that the effects of video games are not uniform and that genre differences exist in both gaming behaviour and its impact on wellbeing, however the effects of genre-level playtime on wellbeing are yet to be studied using digital trace data.

With more than 10,000 new games released each year [@notisYoureRightThere2021], an accessible classification system is essential for studying and comparing video games at scale. Genres, while defined by convention and neither exclusive nor exhaustive as labels [@clarkeWhyVideoGame2017; @starostaTangledWaysClassify2024; @vargas-iglesiasMakingSenseGenre2020], remain the most pragmatic means of categorising video games, providing utility for researchers, players, industry, and policymakers alike. Psychologists have differentiated games based on genre for decades [@griffithsAreComputerGames1993; @wolf6GenreVideo2002], but must negotiate challenges in definition, overlaps between genres, and the continuous evolution of genres as new games are released. Genre labels conflate distinct facets of games, such as gameplay style, purpose, and mood [@leeFacetAnalysisVideo2014]; treating players as pure-genre versus acknowledging multi-genre play alters conclusions about player characteristics [@aziziExperienceMultigenreVideo2018], and factor-analytic decompositions of crowd-sourced game tags produce genre structures that diverge from conventional labels [@liFactororientedUnderstandingVideo2020]. Even the cognitive literature that produced the best-known genre-specific claims now treats genre labels as a weakening proxy for the mechanics that matter, because games increasingly blend mechanics across genres [@bavelierEnhancingAttentionalControl2019]. Genres are therefore best treated not as definitive taxonomical statements but as crude yet practical tools for organising a growing and diversifying library.

There is a lack of consistent standardisation of game genres, therefore classification of video game genres across psychological research is highly inconsistent [@starostaTangledWaysClassify2024]. Of 96 examined articles, only 50 (52%) employ an existing genre classification; 46 (48%) use a unique classification, and 18 (19%) fail to specify the basis or definitions of their genre categorisations altogether. Genre classifications are typically self-reported by participants or assigned by authors, and the same games are habitually classified into different genres across studies. This subjectivity undermines the validity of existing self-report or researcher-ascribed genre taxonomies for the meaningful comparison of results across studies.

Structured, crowd-sourced metadata repositories such as SteamDB, The Games Database, and the Internet Games Database (IGDB) offer a more reliable alternative, involving both game developers and large player samples in collaboratively maintaining genre labels [@liPreliminaryNetworkAnalysis2020; @starostaTangledWaysClassify2024; @leeEmpiricalEvaluationMetadata2015]. Within the constraints of genre as a means of categorising games, metadata repositories best accommodate the fluidity of genres over time [@cohenHistoryGenre1986] and enable comparative research at scale.

## The Present Study

In line with prior evidence [@larrieuHowGamingMotives2023; @ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024; @ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025], our first hypothesis predicts the absence of a meaningful relationship between playtime and wellbeing, this time with digital trace data across several platforms and thousands of games:

**H1.** Total cross-platform playtime is not meaningfully associated with fluctuations in general mental wellbeing over a 2-week period (**H1a**, "within-person") or with average wellbeing over the full study period (**H1b**, "between-person").

We test this via a Bayesian ROPE analysis with equivalence bounds of ±0.06 SWEMWBS item-mean points per hour/day, matching the SESOI used by @ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024. In practical terms, H1a asks whether playing more than one's own average in a given two-week wave is associated with a shift in wellbeing, while H1b asks whether individuals who habitually play more report different average wellbeing than those who play less.

Second, following previous literature [@andreRelationshipGameGenre2024; @dobrowolskiCognitiveEnhancementVideo2015; @raithMassivelyMultiplayerOnline2021; @hazelExploringPossibleMental2022; @elliottContributionGameGenre2012; @rehbeinContributionGameGenre2021], we predict that genres vary in their relation to wellbeing, with some potentially positive and others potentially negative, varying in strength. Put more formally:

**H2.** Genres differ in how playtime relates to fluctuations in general mental wellbeing over a 2-week period (**H2a**, "within-person") and to average wellbeing over the full study period (**H2b**, "between-person").

H2a asks: when a participant plays more than their own average this wave, does it matter what genres that extra playtime is in? H2b asks the between-person complement: among people who play more overall, does it matter whether that habitual extra playtime is concentrated in, for example, RPGs versus Shooters versus other genres? H2 thus tests whether it is justified to generalise video game effects across genres, testing the generalisability that single-title studies must assume [@yarkoniGeneralizabilityCrisis2022].

Beyond the registered hypotheses, we report one unregistered extension. The biweekly window aggregates many individual play sessions into a single retrospective judgement, so the registered tests leave open whether associations operating on shorter timescales are hidden by aggregation. As such, we re-examine both hypotheses at the daily level. This extension was specified after the registered analyses were complete and is reported as exploratory throughout.

    min_date = min(telemetry_files[[p]]$date, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_date = max(telemetry_files[[p]]$date, na.rm = TRUE)

telemetry_range_sentence <- platform_ranges |>
  mutate(platform_range = glue("{platform} ({range_text})")) |>
  pull(platform_range) |>
  paste(collapse = ", ")

intake_range <- intake_raw |>
  summarise(
    min_date = min(date, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_date = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

intake_range_sentence <- glue(
  "{format(intake_range$min_date, '%b %Y')} and {format(intake_range$max_date, '%b %Y')}"
)

## Data Source and Participants

The analyses reported here are part of a Stage 1 Registered Report [@ballou2024psychological], and the data collected for this study are part of the Open Play dataset (v1.2.1) [@ballou2025openplay], a longitudinal dataset that combined multi-platform video game digital trace data alongside daily and biweekly psychological measures from adult gamers in the UK and US over a three-month period. The intake surveys were completed between `r intake_range_sentence`. Digital trace data span the following periods: `r telemetry_range_sentence`.

This study received ethical approval from the Social Sciences and Humanities Inter-Divisional Research Ethics Committee at the University of Oxford (OII_CIA_23_107). All participants provided informed consent at the start of the study, including consent to their data being shared openly for reanalysis.

Participants were paid at an average rate of £12/hour, equating to £0.20 for a 1-minute screening, £2 for the 10-minute intake survey (plus £5 for linking at least one account with recent data), £0.80 for each 4-minute daily survey, and £2 for each 10-minute biweekly survey. Participants received a £10 bonus payment for completing at least 24 out of 30 daily surveys and/or 5 out of 6 biweekly surveys.

```{r}
#| label: build-demographics
#| include: false

# The analytic sample is defined by the models: all participants with at
# least one valid SWEMWBS response in the biweekly survey. Telemetry-based
# playtime is zero for participants/waves without recorded play.
analysis_pids <- read_csv(here("data/clean/survey_biweekly.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(wave >= 1, wave <= 6) |>
  mutate(wemwbs = rowMeans(across(starts_with("wemwbs_")), na.rm = FALSE)) |>
  filter(!is.na(wemwbs)) |>
  distinct(pid) |>
  pull(pid)

n_model <- length(analysis_pids)

genre_matched_pids <- read_csv(here("data/processed/genre_wave_long.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  distinct(pid) |>
  pull(pid)

n_genre_matched <- length(intersect(analysis_pids, genre_matched_pids))

daily_telemetry <- bind_rows(
  read_csv(here("data/clean/xbox.csv.gz"),     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "Xbox"),
  read_csv(here("data/clean/steam.csv.gz"),    show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "Steam"),
  read_csv(here("data/clean/nintendo.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "Nintendo"),
  read_csv(here("data/clean/ios.csv.gz"),      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "iOS"),
  read_csv(here("data/clean/android.csv.gz"),  show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "Android")
) |>
  distinct(pid, platform)

demographics <- intake |>
  filter(qualified) |>
  mutate(
    pid = as.character(pid),
    age_group = cut(
      age,
      breaks = c(17, 24, 30, 35, 40),
      labels = c("18-24", "25-30", "31-35", "36-40")
    ),
    gender = case_when(
      gender %in% c("Man", "Male")     ~ "Man",
      gender %in% c("Woman", "Female") ~ "Woman",
      gender == "Prefer not to say"    ~ NA_character_,
      is.na(gender)                    ~ NA_character_,
      TRUE                             ~ "Non-binary/Other"
    ),
    ethnicity = case_when(
      ethnicity %in% c("White", "White alone")                                          ~ "White",
      ethnicity %in% c("Asian", "Asian alone", "Asian or Asian British")                ~ "Asian",
      ethnicity %in% c("Black", "Black or African American alone",
                       "Black, African, Caribbean or Black British")                    ~ "Black",
      ethnicity %in% c("Mixed", "Mixed or multiple ethnic groups", "Two or More Races") ~ "Mixed/Multiple",
      ethnicity == "Prefer not to say"                                                  ~ NA_character_,
      is.na(ethnicity)                                                                  ~ NA_character_,
      TRUE                                                                              ~ "Other"
    )
  ) |>
  select(pid, country, age, age_group, gender, ethnicity)

analytic_sample <- demographics |>
  filter(pid %in% analysis_pids, !is.na(age_group))

n_total <- nrow(analytic_sample)
n_us    <- sum(analytic_sample$country == "US", na.rm = TRUE)
n_uk    <- sum(analytic_sample$country == "UK", na.rm = TRUE)

n_intake_total <- nrow(intake)
n_qualified    <- sum(intake$qualified, na.rm = TRUE)
```

# prose reads `r name` rather than a formatting call.
txt_n_intake_total <- formatC(n_intake_total, format = "d", big.mark = ",")

```

From `r txt_n_intake_total` participants who completed the intake survey, `r txt_n_qualified` met the preregistered screening and linking criteria. The analytic sample comprises the `r txt_n_model` participants who provided valid SWEMWBS responses in at least one biweekly survey wave. Playtime for these participants is measured from their linked Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam accounts; participants and waves without recorded play on these platforms are retained with zero hours rather than excluded, and `r txt_n_genre_matched` participants (`r txt_pct_genre_matched`%) had at least one gameplay session of a game that could be matched to a genre. The demographic sensitivity analysis uses the `r txt_n_total` participants with a matching qualified intake record and age within the 18-40 screening range (`r txt_n_us` US, `r txt_n_uk` UK; mean age `r txt_mean_age` years, `r txt_pct_men`% men); `r txt_n_excluded_demo` analytic-sample participants are excluded from that subset (`r txt_n_no_intake_record` without a matching intake record, `r txt_n_over_40` aged over 40). Full demographic characteristics, including country-level breakdowns, are reported in @tbl-demographics.

```{r}
#| label: genre-metadata-stats
#| include: false

# --- Raw IGDB label statistics (game_metadata.csv.gz) -----------------------
meta_raw_gm   <- read_csv(here("data/clean/game_metadata.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)
meta_labelled <- meta_raw_gm |> filter(!is.na(genres), nchar(genres) > 0)
raw_label_list      <- map(str_split(meta_labelled$genres, ","), str_trim)
raw_labels_distinct <- sort(unique(unlist(raw_label_list)))
n_raw_genre_labels  <- length(raw_labels_distinct)
n_labels_per_game   <- lengths(raw_label_list)
max_raw_labels      <- max(n_labels_per_game)
pct_games_gt3_labels <- 100 * mean(n_labels_per_game > 3)

# Genre count under the PRE-REGISTERED collapsing (for Appendix B)
prereg_collapse <- function(g) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    g == "Hack and slash/Beat 'em up" ~ "Action",
    g %in% c("Turn-based strategy (TBS)", "Real Time Strategy (RTS)", "Tactical") ~ "Strategy",
    g %in% c("Point-and-click", "Visual Novel") ~ "Adventure",
    g == "Quiz/Trivia" ~ "Puzzle",
    TRUE ~ g
  )
}
n_prereg_genres <- n_distinct(prereg_collapse(raw_labels_distinct))

# --- Xbox genre coverage before/after the local mapping fix. Computed for
# reference only; the fix is ordinary data cleaning and is no longer reported
# in the text or catalogued as a deviation.
meta_fixed_gm <- populate_xbox_genres(meta_raw_gm)
xb_has <- function(meta) meta |> filter(platform == "Xbox") |>
  transmute(original_name, has = !is.na(genres) & nchar(genres) > 0)
xbox_cov <- telemetry_files$Xbox |>
  left_join(xb_has(meta_raw_gm),   by = c("title_id" = "original_name")) |>
  rename(has_before = has) |>
  left_join(xb_has(meta_fixed_gm), by = c("title_id" = "original_name")) |>
  rename(has_after = has) |>
  summarise(
    total_min  = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_before = sum(duration[replace_na(has_before, FALSE)], na.rm = TRUE),
    min_after  = sum(duration[replace_na(has_after,  FALSE)], na.rm = TRUE)
  )
xbox_pct_before  <- 100 * xbox_cov$min_before / xbox_cov$total_min
xbox_pct_after   <- 100 * xbox_cov$min_after  / xbox_cov$total_min
xbox_min_rescued <- xbox_cov$min_after - xbox_cov$min_before

# --- In-study (waves 1-6) sessions, from the already-loaded telemetry -------
survey_ms   <- load_survey_data() |> filter(wave >= 1, wave <= 6)
sessions_ms <- bind_rows(
  telemetry_files$Nintendo |> transmute(pid, platform = "Nintendo", title_id, date, duration),
  telemetry_files$Xbox     |> transmute(pid, platform = "Xbox",     title_id, date, duration),
  telemetry_files$Steam    |> transmute(pid, platform = "Steam",    title_id, date, duration = minutes)
)
sessions_instudy <- add_waves(sessions_ms, survey_ms)

# Distinct in-study titles for the analytic sample (quoted in the abstract;
# pinned in abstract-claims-guard)
n_titles_instudy <- sessions_instudy |>
  filter(pid %in% analysis_pids) |>
  distinct(title_id, platform) |>
  nrow()

# Genre coverage of in-study playtime and platform composition (for Methods
# and Limitations): share of minutes matched to >= 1 study genre
matched_keys_ms <- load_game_metadata_long() |> distinct(original_name, platform)
cov_by_platform <- sessions_instudy |>
  left_join(matched_keys_ms |> mutate(matched = TRUE),
            by = c("title_id" = "original_name", "platform")) |>
  mutate(matched = replace_na(matched, FALSE)) |>
  group_by(platform) |>
  summarise(minutes = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
            pct_matched = 100 * sum(duration[matched], na.rm = TRUE) / minutes,
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(share = 100 * minutes / sum(minutes))
genre_cov_overall <- with(cov_by_platform, 100 * sum(minutes * pct_matched / 100) / sum(minutes))
cov_get   <- function(p) cov_by_platform$pct_matched[cov_by_platform$platform == p]
share_get <- function(p) cov_by_platform$share[cov_by_platform$platform == p]

# --- Telemetry history depth and wave-1 behaviour/availability --------------
# All rates below use the analytic sample as their basis: play rates are
# per analytic-sample participant; availability is per analytic-sample
# participant with any telemetry on the platform.
first_dates_ms <- sessions_ms |>
  filter(pid %in% analysis_pids) |>
  group_by(pid, platform) |>
  summarise(first_date = min(date, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  inner_join(survey_ms |> distinct(pid, baseline_date), by = "pid") |>
  mutate(days_before = as.numeric(baseline_date - first_date))
med_days <- first_dates_ms |>
  group_by(platform) |>
  summarise(median_days = median(days_before), .groups = "drop") |>
  (\(d) setNames(d$median_days, d$platform))()

w1_played <- sessions_instudy |>
  filter(wave == 1, pid %in% analysis_pids) |>
  distinct(pid, platform)
w1_rate   <- function(p) 100 * sum(w1_played$platform == p) / n_model
# Availability: telemetry history covers the full wave-1 window
w1_avail <- first_dates_ms |>
  mutate(covers_w1 = days_before >= 14) |>
  group_by(platform) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(covers_w1), .groups = "drop") |>
  (\(d) setNames(d$pct, d$platform))()

# Guard for the fixed prose: full-window telemetry availability is high on
# every platform among linked participants.
stopifnot(all(w1_avail[c("Nintendo", "Xbox", "Steam")] >= 80))
```

#| label: load-mobile

survey <- load_survey_data()
baselines <- survey |> distinct(pid, baseline_date)

ios     <- read_csv(here("data/clean/ios.csv.gz"),     show_col_types = FALSE)
android <- read_csv(here("data/clean/android.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)

mobile <- bind_rows(ios, android) |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(day_local)) |>
  group_by(pid, date) |>
  summarise(minutes = sum(minutes, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(baselines, by = "pid") |>
  filter(!is.na(baseline_date)) |>
  mutate(wave = assign_wave_vec(date, baseline_date)) |>
  filter(!is.na(wave), wave >= 1, wave <= 6) |>
  group_by(pid, wave) |>
  summarise(mobile_hours_per_day = sum(minutes, na.rm = TRUE) / 60 / 14,
            .groups = "drop")

# Merge mobile into total_playtime (no double-counting; console/PC side comes
# from raw sessions via 01_preprocess.R)
total_playtime <- total_playtime |>
  left_join(mobile, by = c("pid", "wave")) |>
  mutate(
    mobile_hours_per_day     = replace_na(mobile_hours_per_day, 0),
    total_time_all_platforms = total_hours_per_day + mobile_hours_per_day
  ) |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  mutate(
    total_time_all_platforms_within  = total_time_all_platforms - mean(total_time_all_platforms, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_time_all_platforms_between = mean(total_time_all_platforms, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

```{r}
#| label: build-aggregated-playtime
#| include: false

# Build wide-format aggregated_playtime and genre variable vectors from the
# new long-format pipeline (genre_wave_long + total_playtime + survey).
#
# Sanitize genre names to valid R column names, e.g.:
#   "Action & Adventure"  → "time_action_adventure"
#   "Role-playing (RPG)"  → "time_role_playing_rpg"
#   "Shooter"             → "time_shooter"
genre_to_col <- function(g) {
  col <- gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "_", tolower(g))
  col <- gsub("^_+|_+$", "", col)
  paste0("time_", col)
}

# Pivot genre_wave_long wide: one time_{genre} column per genre per pid × wave.
# values_fill = 0 handles genre × wave combos with no play.
genre_wide <- genre_wave_long |>
  mutate(col = genre_to_col(genre)) |>
  select(pid, wave, col, hours_per_day) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = hours_per_day, values_fill = 0)

genre_vars <- sort(setdiff(names(genre_wide), c("pid", "wave")))

# Build aggregated_playtime starting from the full survey (includes 0-play waves).
# Left-joining telemetry ensures participants who skipped gaming in a wave get 0.
aggregated_playtime <- survey |>
  select(pid, wave, wemwbs, self_reported_biweekly_play) |>
  left_join(
    total_playtime |> select(pid, wave, total_hours_per_day,
                             mobile_hours_per_day, total_time_all_platforms),
    by = c("pid", "wave")
  ) |>
  left_join(genre_wide, by = c("pid", "wave")) |>
  mutate(
    total_time_all_genres    = replace_na(total_hours_per_day, 0),
    mobile_hours_per_day     = replace_na(mobile_hours_per_day, 0),
    total_time_all_platforms = replace_na(total_time_all_platforms, 0),
    across(all_of(genre_vars), ~ replace_na(.x, 0))
  ) |>
  select(-total_hours_per_day) |>
  # Within/between decompose over ALL survey waves (including 0-play waves)
  group_by(pid) |>
  mutate(
    total_time_all_platforms_within  =
      total_time_all_platforms - mean(total_time_all_platforms, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_time_all_platforms_between =
      mean(total_time_all_platforms, na.rm = TRUE),
    across(
      all_of(genre_vars),
      list(
        within  = ~ .x - mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        between = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

genre_within_vars  <- paste0(genre_vars, "_within")
genre_between_vars <- paste0(genre_vars, "_between")
genre_vars_demean  <- c(genre_within_vars, genre_between_vars)

## Measures

The distributions and structure of the key variables are visualised in @fig-descriptives.

```{r}
#| label: swemwbs-reliability
#| include: false

# Internal consistency of the 7 SWEMWBS items over all analytic person-waves
# (McDonald's omega total and Cronbach's alpha; psych). Reported in Measures.
swemwbs_items <- read_csv(here("data/clean/survey_biweekly.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(pid %in% analysis_pids, wave >= 1, wave <= 6) |>
  select(starts_with("wemwbs_")) |>
  drop_na()
stopifnot(ncol(swemwbs_items) == 7)
swemwbs_omega <- suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
  psych::omega(swemwbs_items, nfactors = 1, plot = FALSE)))$omega.tot
swemwbs_alpha <- suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(psych::alpha(swemwbs_items)))$total$raw_alpha
stopifnot(swemwbs_omega > 0.8, swemwbs_alpha > 0.8)
```

```{r}
#| label: txt-measures-1
#| include: false

# Inline quantities for the paragraph(s) below, defined once here so the
# prose reads `r name` rather than a formatting call.
txt_swemwbs_omega <- sprintf("%.2f", swemwbs_omega)
txt_swemwbs_alpha <- sprintf("%.2f", swemwbs_alpha)
```

**Wellbeing.** Wellbeing was assessed using the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale (SWEMWBS) [@tennant2007warwick], a 7-item short form of the WEMWBS covering psychological functioning and subjective wellbeing over the past 2 weeks, with responses on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from "None of the time" to "All of the time." Scores are computed as the arithmetic mean of the 7 items (range: 1–5). Internal consistency across all analytic person-waves was high (McDonald's ω~t~ = `r txt_swemwbs_omega`, Cronbach's α = `r txt_swemwbs_alpha`). All reported coefficients, priors, and the preregistered SESOI are defined on this item-mean scale.

**Video game playtime.** Digital trace data from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam provide session-level records (per-title start and end timestamps), while iOS and Android contribute only daily aggregate minutes (no game-level metadata). Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam therefore contribute to both H1 (total playtime) and H2 (genre-specific playtime); iOS and Android contribute only to the preregistered all-platform sensitivity analysis (Appendix A, Deviation D4).

```{r}
#| label: genre-upset-data
#| include: false

# Filter to only games played by participants in the analysis.
# telemetry_genre (loaded above) contains wave-assigned sessions for study
# participants; semi_join restricts meta_long_full to those title_ids only.
relevant_games <- telemetry_genre |> distinct(title_id, platform)

# Build combination labels and playtime per game-platform pair
game_combos <- meta_long_full |>
  semi_join(relevant_games, by = c("original_name" = "title_id", "platform")) |>
  distinct(original_name, platform, genre) |>
  group_by(original_name, platform) |>
  summarise(combination = paste(sort(genre), collapse = " + "), .groups = "drop")

n_total_games <- nrow(game_combos)

# Total playtime per game-platform pair.
# telemetry_genre is genre-long (one row per session x genre label), so a
# k-genre game's sessions appear k times; divide by the game's label count
# to recover true playtime. Within a game the label set is constant.
game_hours <- telemetry_genre |>
  group_by(title_id, platform) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE) / 60 / n_distinct(genre),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Summary statistics for the co-occurrence prose in Measures
cooc_stats <- game_combos |>
  left_join(game_hours, by = c("original_name" = "title_id", "platform")) |>
  mutate(
    total_hours = replace_na(total_hours, 0),
    multi = str_detect(combination, fixed(" + "))
  ) |>
  summarise(
    n_combinations       = n_distinct(combination),
    pct_multigenre_games = 100 * mean(multi),
    pct_multigenre_hours = 100 * sum(total_hours[multi]) / sum(total_hours)
  )
n_combinations       <- cooc_stats$n_combinations
pct_multigenre_games <- cooc_stats$pct_multigenre_games
pct_multigenre_hours <- cooc_stats$pct_multigenre_hours

# --- Data for playtime-weighted UpSet plot (exact hours) ---
# Compute exact total hours per genre intersection
int_hours <- game_combos |>
  left_join(game_hours, by = c("original_name" = "title_id", "platform")) |>
  mutate(total_hours = replace_na(total_hours, 0)) |>
  group_by(combination) |>
  summarise(hours = sum(total_hours), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(hours)) |>
  slice_head(n = 40) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number())

# Parse each combination into its constituent genres
int_genres <- int_hours |>
  mutate(genres_list = str_split(combination, " \\+ ")) |>
  unnest(genres_list) |>
  rename(genre = genres_list)

# All genres appearing in the top intersections (ordered by total hours across
# all games, ascending so the most common genre appears at the top of the matrix)
genre_totals <- game_combos |>
  left_join(game_hours, by = c("original_name" = "title_id", "platform")) |>
  mutate(total_hours = replace_na(total_hours, 0)) |>
  mutate(genres_list = str_split(combination, " \\+ ")) |>
  unnest(genres_list) |>
  group_by(genre = genres_list) |>
  summarise(genre_hours = sum(total_hours), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(genre_hours)

genre_order <- genre_totals$genre

# Dot matrix: which genres are active for each intersection
dot_df <- expand_grid(rank = int_hours$rank, genre = genre_order) |>
  left_join(int_genres |> select(rank, genre) |> mutate(active = TRUE),
            by = c("rank", "genre")) |>
  mutate(active = replace_na(active, FALSE),
         genre = factor(genre, levels = genre_order))

# Connecting segments between active dots in multi-genre intersections
seg_df <- int_genres |>
  mutate(ypos = match(genre, genre_order)) |>
  group_by(rank) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>
  summarise(
    ymin = genre_order[min(ypos)],
    ymax = genre_order[max(ypos)],
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: txt-measures-2
#| include: false

# Inline quantities for the paragraph(s) below, defined once here so the
# prose reads `r name` rather than a formatting call.
txt_genre_cov_overall <- round(genre_cov_overall, 1)
txt_cov_get_Steam <- round(cov_get("Steam"), 1)
txt_cov_get_Nintendo <- round(cov_get("Nintendo"), 1)
txt_cov_get_Xbox <- round(cov_get("Xbox"), 1)
txt_n_total_games <- formatC(n_total_games, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
txt_pct_multigenre_games <- round(pct_multigenre_games)
```

**Game genre classification.** Game genre labels for Nintendo and Steam are obtained by cross-referencing game titles in the digital trace data with the Internet Games Database (IGDB). IGDB is, to our knowledge, the only database with complete multi-platform metadata coverage that offers an API for programmatic data retrieval. The genre labels are crowd-sourced: community members can submit contributions (e.g., a new game or alternative categorisation), which are vetted by admins and moderators before appearing in the database. For Xbox, game titles could not be matched to IGDB genre labels, since Xbox provided us only with anonymised title identifiers. Instead, genre labels were available through the Xbox store and were mapped onto the IGDB taxonomy. In total, we collected `r n_raw_genre_labels` distinct raw IGDB genre labels, converted the Xbox store genres into the IGDB taxonomy, and collapsed them into 14 study-level genre categories (e.g., Strategy subsumes Turn-Based Strategy (TBS), Real-Time Strategy (RTS), Tactical, and MOBA; Puzzle subsumes Card & Board Game and Quiz/Trivia). The complete mapping table can be found in Appendix B, and the descriptive statistics by genre in Appendix C. We did not consider IGDB "themes" or other metadata fields. Overall, `r txt_genre_cov_overall`% of in-study playtime is matched to at least one study genre (Steam `r txt_cov_get_Steam`%, Nintendo `r txt_cov_get_Nintendo`%, Xbox `r txt_cov_get_Xbox`%), with unmatched playtime counting towards the total playtime but towards no genre.

**Genre co-occurrence and compositional multi-genre attribution.** Across the `r txt_n_total_games` individual games in our dataset, `r txt_pct_multigenre_games`% carry more than one genre label, leading to `r n_combinations` distinct genre combinations. @fig-genre-upset shows the playtime-weighted co-occurrence structure across the 40 most-played combinations, and @tbl-genre-cooccurrence lists the ten most-played combinations with their top titles. Operationalising games as multi-genre has consequential effects in relation to playtime and can be handled in one of three ways, which differ in how they construct the genre-exposure variable and how they enter the models.

*Partial attribution* splits a session's playtime across its genres. A 60-minute session of *Skyrim* (Adventure and RPG) would be allocated as 30 minutes of Adventure and 30 minutes of RPG (or potentially a different, unequal partition). This preserves the constraint that exposure sums to total playtime but penalises multi-genre games, since the more genres a game carries, the less exposure it contributes to each, even though the game belongs fully to each genre, not partially.

*Full attribution* counts a session's full duration towards every genre it carries. The same 60-minute *Skyrim* session counts as 60 minutes of Adventure and 60 minutes of RPG. Consider a person who plays 60 minutes of *Skyrim* (Adventure + RPG) and 60 minutes of *Final Fantasy XIV Online* (RPG only). Under partial attribution, *Skyrim* contributes 30 minutes to each genre, yielding 30 total minutes of Adventure and 90 minutes of RPG, a 1:3 ratio implying three times as much RPG engagement as Adventure. Under full attribution, *Skyrim* contributes 60 minutes to each genre, yielding 60 minutes of Adventure and 120 minutes of RPG, a 2:1 ratio that better reflects that RPG-labelled content received twice the engagement of Adventure-labelled content. A consequence is that genre exposures no longer sum to total playtime. Genre-level coefficients therefore represent the association with an added hour of that genre's exposure holding total playtime constant, for example, replacing a single-genre RPG session with a dual-genre Adventure/RPG session of the same length.

*Proportional multi-membership weighting* converts full attribution hours to compositional weights by dividing each genre's exposure hours by total exposure (e.g., 33.3% Adventure, 66.7% RPG for a wave consisting of 60 minutes of *Skyrim* and 60 minutes of *Final Fantasy XIV Online*) and uses these as multi-membership weights on a single total-playtime slope. Genre does not enter the model (M4) as an independent predictor of wellbeing but as a modifier of the playtime–wellbeing slope. Thus, a wave consisting mostly of RPG play has its playtime coefficient adjusted mostly by the RPG slope modifier, with other genres contributing in proportion to their share of that wave's play. This weighting shares a limitation with partial attribution: adding a genre label to a game lowers the shares of the labels it already carries, so none of the three options is free of trade-offs. The genre-specific slope adjustments are drawn from a common distribution whose standard deviation, σ~s~, is M4's answer to H2.

::: {.place arguments="top, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-genre-upset
#| fig-cap: "*Genre Co-Occurrence Weighted by Total Playtime.* Top panel: total hours played by games in each genre combination, ordered by playtime. Bottom panel: dot matrix indicating which genres belong to each combination; connected dots denote multi-genre games. Left bars show total hours attributed to each genre, counting a multi-genre game's full playtime towards each genre exposure."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false

# Shared 14-genre palette (pal_genre, keyed on display names) applied to the
# genre bars and matrix dots; map this figure's raw genre names to display.
col_for_genre <- function(g) {
  disp <- ifelse(g %in% names(raw_to_display), unname(raw_to_display[g]), g)
  unname(pal_genre[disp])
}
stopifnot(!any(is.na(col_for_genre(as.character(genre_totals$genre)))))

# Top panel: bar chart of exact hours per intersection
p_bars <- ggplot(int_hours, aes(x = rank, y = hours)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey30", width = 0.35) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = int_hours$rank, expand = expansion(add = 0.5)) +
  labs(y = "Total hours played") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x  = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    plot.margin  = margin(2, 5, 0, 5)
  )

# Bottom panel: dot-and-line matrix
p_matrix <- ggplot(dot_df |>
                     mutate(colour_key = ifelse(active, as.character(genre), "inactive")),
                   aes(x = rank, y = genre)) +
  geom_segment(data = seg_df,
               aes(x = rank, xend = rank, y = ymin, yend = ymax),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = colour_key, size = active), show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    setNames(col_for_genre(unique(as.character(dot_df$genre))),
             unique(as.character(dot_df$genre))),
    inactive = "grey85"
  )) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c("TRUE" = 1.8, "FALSE" = 0.8)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = int_hours$rank, expand = expansion(add = 0.5)) +
  labs(y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x  = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y  = element_blank(),
    panel.grid   = element_blank(),
    plot.margin  = margin(0, 5, 2, 5)
  )

# Left panel: genre totals (horizontal bars), shared 14-genre palette
p_genre <- ggplot(genre_totals |> mutate(genre = factor(genre, levels = genre_order)),
                  aes(x = genre_hours, y = genre, fill = genre)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.35) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(col_for_genre(as.character(genre_totals$genre)),
                                      as.character(genre_totals$genre)),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_x_reverse(labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k", accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_discrete(position = "right") +
  labs(x = "Hours per genre") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    plot.margin  = margin(0, 0, 2, 5)
  )

# Compose: left genre bars aligned with the dot matrix; bars on top
# Use patchwork: flat 2x2 grid so columns align across rows
p_spacer <- plot_spacer()

p_spacer + p_bars + p_genre + p_matrix +
  plot_layout(
    design = "AB\nCD",
    heights = c(3, 2),
    widths  = c(1, 4)
  )

#| label: tbl-genre-cooccurrence
#| tbl-cap: "Top 10 genre combinations by total playtime. Multi-genre rows join labels with ' + '. Total hours = playtime for games with that combination; % of playtime = share of all genre-matched playtime; n games = unique game-platform pairs. Xbox titles are anonymised."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| echo: false

# Session-level stats per combination.
# telemetry_genre already has display_name from the genre-descriptives-extended chunk.
# Deflate genre-long rows by each game's label count (see game_hours above)
# so per-title minutes count each session once.
title_min <- telemetry_genre |>
  left_join(game_combos, by = c("title_id" = "original_name", "platform")) |>
  filter(!is.na(combination)) |>
  group_by(combination, title_id, display_name) |>
  summarise(total_min = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE) / n_distinct(genre),
            .groups = "drop")

total_matched_minutes <- sum(title_min$total_min)

combo_stats <- title_min |>
  group_by(combination) |>
  mutate(
    combo_total = sum(total_min),
    pct_title   = round(100 * total_min / combo_total, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_min)) |>
  summarise(
    n_games          = n(),
    total_minutes    = first(combo_total),
    mean_min_per_day = first(combo_total) / total_person_days,
    top_5 = paste(
      paste0(display_name[1:min(5, n())], " [", pct_title[1:min(5, n())], "%]"),
      collapse = ", "
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_minutes)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(
    `% of playtime` = round(100 * total_minutes / total_matched_minutes, 1)
  ) |>
  transmute(
    `Genre combination` = gsub("[()]", "", gsub("Role-playing (RPG)", "Role-playing", combination, fixed = TRUE)),
    `Total hours`       = round(total_minutes / 60, 1),
    `% of playtime`,
    `n games`           = n_games,
    `Mean min/day`      = round(mean_min_per_day, 1),
    `Top 5 titles`      = replace_na(top_5, "")
  )

combo_stats |>
  tt(width = c(0.20, 0.09, 0.10, 0.08, 0.09, 0.44)) |>
  format_tt(digits = 1) |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.8) |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)

(B) Average daily hours per person-wave with recorded play (15-minute bins; dashed line: median). (C) Share of recorded playtime per study day by platform, days 1\u201384. Two outcomes are overlaid on the right axis: biweekly SWEMWBS (purple open squares, 1\u20135) at each survey date, and daily life satisfaction from the 30-day diary (red open circles, 0\u2013100).")'

desc_svy <- survey |> filter(pid %in% analysis_pids)

pct_zero_pw <- 100 * mean(pw$total_hours_per_day == 0)

# Panel A: SWEMWBS by wave (raincloud: density + raw points + median box),
# fill lightening across waves 1-6.
panel_a <- desc_svy |>
  filter(!is.na(wemwbs)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(wave), y = wemwbs, fill = factor(wave))) +

# Panel B: distribution of the playtime dose (15-minute bins; median marked)

med_dose <- median(pw_pos$total_hours_per_day)

# Panel C: platform share of recorded playtime across study days

  mutate(prop = minutes / sum(minutes)) |>
  ungroup()

panel_c <- ggplot(plat_daily, aes(x = study_day, y = prop, fill = platform)) +

  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Nintendo = "#D55E00", Steam = "#0072B2", Xbox = "#009E73")) +

# Panel D: one participant (75th percentile of playtime), day by day, with
# each day represented the way M4 represents a wave: bar height = clock time
# of genre-matched play, segments = w_g * total, where w_g = full-attribution
# genre minutes / their sum (proportional multi-membership weighting,
# Methods). Days are counted from baseline (day 0); waves 1-6 are the 14-day
# blocks ending on the survey days (days -14..69), marked by dashed lines.
daily_genre_telemetry <- load_genre_sessions(meta_long_full) |>
  group_by(pid, platform, title_id, date) |>
  mutate(n_labels = n_distinct(genre)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  group_by(pid, date, genre) |>
  summarise(minutes_full  = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
            minutes_clock = sum(duration / n_labels, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(day_local = date) |>
  mutate(genre_display = if_else(genre %in% names(raw_to_display),
                                 unname(raw_to_display[genre]), genre))

dgs <- daily_genre_telemetry |>
  inner_join(study_starts, by = "pid") |>
  mutate(study_day = as.integer(day_local - study_start)) |>
  filter(study_day >= -14, study_day <= 69)

eligible_cs <- desc_svy |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  summarise(n_surveys = sum(!is.na(wemwbs)), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_surveys >= 3)

tot_by_pid <- dgs |>
  semi_join(eligible_cs, by = "pid") |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  summarise(total_minutes = sum(minutes_clock),
            n_genres = n_distinct(genre), .groups = "drop")

# Shown participant: chosen for informativeness (recorded play in every wave,
# many genres, both outcomes observed). p_show_pct records where they sit in
# the distribution of genre-matched playtime (no longer quoted in the caption).
p75_pid <- "p5271179686"
stopifnot(p75_pid %in% tot_by_pid$pid)
p_show_pct <- round(100 * mean(tot_by_pid$total_minutes <=
                                 tot_by_pid$total_minutes[tot_by_pid$pid == p75_pid]))

# Daily diary (life satisfaction 0-100; completion is UTC, utc_offset in hours)
daily_lite <- read_csv(here("data/processed/daily/daily_model_frame.csv"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(pid, completion, utc_offset, life_sat)

outcome_cols <- c(wb = "#5E3C99", ls = "#C1272D")
outcome_labs <- c(wb = "SWEMWBS", ls = "Daily life satisfaction")
wave_edges   <- seq(-14.5, 69.5, by = 14)

# Panel D builder: one participant, days -14..69 from baseline, bars = clock
# time of genre-matched play composed with M4's proportional weights, SWEMWBS
# and daily life satisfaction overlaid on a shared right axis (0-100 mapped
# linearly onto 1-5). Legend lists only the genres this participant played.
make_panel_d <- function(pid_sel, title = "One Participant in Full") {
  cs_day <- dgs |>
    filter(pid == pid_sel) |>
    group_by(study_day) |>
    mutate(total_clock = sum(minutes_clock),
           w = minutes_full / sum(minutes_full)) |>
    ungroup() |>
    transmute(study_day, g = genre_display, w, minutes = w * total_clock)

  cs_grid <- expand_grid(study_day = -14:69, g = rank14) |>
    left_join(cs_day, by = c("study_day", "g")) |>
    mutate(w = replace_na(w, 0), minutes = replace_na(minutes, 0),
           g = factor(g, levels = rank14))

  # Guards: shares sum to 1 on every day with play; stacked bars are clock time
  w_check <- cs_grid |> group_by(study_day) |> summarise(w = sum(w), m = sum(minutes))
  stopifnot(all(abs(w_check$w[w_check$w > 0] - 1) < 1e-6), max(w_check$m) <= 24 * 60)
  played <- cs_grid |> group_by(g) |> summarise(m = sum(minutes)) |>
    filter(m > 0) |> pull(g) |> as.character()

  # Biweekly survey timestamps are UTC; convert to the participant's local date
  # using their modal UTC offset from the daily diary (0 if not in the diary).
  cs_offset <- daily_lite |> filter(pid == pid_sel) |>
    count(utc_offset, sort = TRUE) |> slice_head(n = 1) |> pull(utc_offset)
  if (length(cs_offset) == 0) cs_offset <- 0
  cs_wb <- desc_svy |>
    filter(pid == pid_sel, !is.na(wemwbs)) |>
    inner_join(study_starts, by = "pid") |>
    mutate(local_date = as.Date(as.POSIXct(date, tz = "UTC") + cs_offset * 3600, tz = "UTC"),
           study_day  = as.integer(local_date - study_start)) |>
    select(study_day, wemwbs)
  cs_daily <- daily_lite |>
    filter(pid == pid_sel, !is.na(life_sat)) |>
    inner_join(study_starts, by = "pid") |>
    mutate(local_date = as.Date(completion + utc_offset * 3600, tz = "UTC"),
           study_day  = as.integer(local_date - study_start)) |>
    filter(study_day >= -14, study_day <= 69) |>
    select(study_day, life_sat)

  coeff_cs <- max(w_check$m) / 4
  x_max_d  <- max(70.5, max(cs_wb$study_day, -Inf) + 0.5)
  x_scale_d <- scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-14.5, x_max_d), breaks = seq(-14, 70, 14),
                                  expand = c(0.01, 0))

  ggplot() +
    geom_col(data = cs_grid, aes(x = study_day, y = minutes, fill = g), width = 1) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = wave_edges, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
    annotate("text", x = wave_edges[-7] + 7, y = max(w_check$m) * 1.04,
             label = paste("Wave", 1:6), size = 4, colour = "grey30") +
    geom_line(data = cs_daily,
              aes(x = study_day, y = life_sat / 25 * coeff_cs, colour = "ls"),
              linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(data = cs_daily,
               aes(x = study_day, y = life_sat / 25 * coeff_cs, colour = "ls", shape = "ls"),
               fill = "white", size = 2.1, stroke = 0.9) +
    geom_line(data = cs_wb,
              aes(x = study_day, y = (wemwbs - 1) * coeff_cs, colour = "wb"),
              linewidth = 1.1) +
    geom_point(data = cs_wb,
               aes(x = study_day, y = (wemwbs - 1) * coeff_cs, colour = "wb", shape = "wb"),
               fill = "white", size = 2.6, stroke = 1.1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = outcome_cols, labels = outcome_labs, name = NULL,
                        limits = c("wb", "ls"), drop = FALSE) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(wb = 22, ls = 21), labels = outcome_labs, name = NULL,
                       limits = c("wb", "ls"), drop = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = pal_genre, name = NULL, breaks = played) +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(order = 1, ncol = 1,
                                 override.aes = list(shape = c(22, 21), fill = "white",
                                                     size = c(2.6, 2.1), linewidth = c(1.1, 0.7))),
           shape  = "none",
           fill   = guide_legend(nrow = 2, order = 2)) +
    x_scale_d +
    scale_y_continuous(
      "Daily playtime (minutes)",
      sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / coeff_cs + 1,
                          name = sprintf("<span style='color:%s'>SWEMWBS</span>  |  <span style='color:%s'>Daily life satisfaction</span>",
                                         outcome_cols[["wb"]], outcome_cols[["ls"]]),
                          breaks = 1:5,
                          labels = function(b) sprintf(
                            "<span style='color:%s'>%s</span> | <span style='color:%s'>%s</span>",
                            outcome_cols[["wb"]], b, outcome_cols[["ls"]], (b - 1) * 25))
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Days from baseline", tag = "D") +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "horizontal",
      legend.box.just = "top",
      legend.key.size = unit(4, "mm"), legend.key.spacing.x = unit(3, "mm"),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
      legend.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0), legend.spacing.x = unit(2, "mm"),
      axis.title.y.right = ggtext::element_markdown(angle = 90),
      axis.text.y.right  = ggtext::element_markdown(),
      axis.ticks.y.right = element_line(colour = "grey40")
    )
}

panel_d <- make_panel_d(p75_pid)

p_descriptives <- ((panel_a + labs(tag = "A") | panel_b + labs(tag = "B") |
                    panel_c + labs(tag = "C")) / panel_d) +
  patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.15)) &
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.tag = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", margin = margin(b = 4)),
        plot.margin = margin(4, 6, 2, 4))

p_descriptives
```
:::

## Analytic Approach

All analyses were conducted in R [@rcoreteamLanguageEnvironmentStatistical2025], and the manuscript was written in Quarto [@allaireQuarto2025]. We fit four Bayesian multilevel models with `brms` [@burkner2017brms] at the biweekly timescale, and refit each at the daily timescale as an exploratory extension. Two were preregistered: the random-effects within-between (REWB) regression of total playtime (M1) tests H1, and the genre model with independently estimated genre coefficients (M2) tests H2. Two are exploratory and were added after the M2 results were known: M3 keeps M2's predictors but pools the genre coefficients through a common prior, whereas M4 keeps total playtime as the single predictor, as in M1, and lets each wave's genre composition modify its slope; both answer H2 through the estimated spread of genre effects, and M4 also yields H1 estimates. The Results are organised by hypothesis; within each, the preregistered model comes first and the exploratory models second, and every figure row, legend entry, and table row is labelled by model with its registration status. Deviations from the preregistered plan are catalogued in Appendix A and are flagged below where they affect interpretation.

## Smallest Effect Size of Interest

Establishing the absence of a practically significant effect requires committing in advance to a threshold below which an association is too small to matter, the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI). By practically significant, we mean the smallest change in wellbeing that a player would themselves notice, known also as a minimally important difference (MID). Following previous studies, the MID is set at 0.3 points on the 1–5 SWEMWBS scale, converging with anchor-based estimates of the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale (WEMWBS) [@ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024; @maheswaranEvaluatingResponsivenessWarwick2012] and the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) [@anvari2021anchor].

To calculate the SESOI, we also need to know how large a change in playtime is realistically available to reach the MID. Because UK and US adults average approximately 5 hours of daily leisure time [@sturmFreeTimePhysical2019], this provides us with an upper bound on how much daily play could plausibly rise or fall without it displacing other behaviours that arguably impact wellbeing more than play (e.g., sleep). SESOI is the ratio of the two: 0.3 ÷ 5 = 0.06 points per hour. An association smaller than this means that even a person who shifted their entire 5-hour daily leisure time budget into or out of gaming would not experience a noticeable change in wellbeing.

We evaluate all individual coefficients (H1) against the interval between the negative and positive SESOI \[−0.06, +0.06\], also known as the Region of Practical Equivalence (ROPE) [@kruschke2018rejecting]. If a coefficient's 95% credible interval (CrI) falls entirely inside the ROPE, the effect is considered practically null, meaning even the largest plausible effect is too small to matter; a CrI entirely beyond either bound indicates a practically positive or negative effect, and one straddling either edge is inconclusive.

Evaluating genre heterogeneity (H2) requires a modified rule, because it represents a spread of differences rather than a single effect. We consider genre differences to be practically negligible only if 95% of the genre-specific effects fall inside the ROPE. Because 95% of a normal distribution lies within ±1.96 standard deviations of the centre, fitting this distribution inside our 0.06 ROPE requires the spread (standard deviation) to be below 0.031 (0.06 ÷ 1.96). If the posterior probability of meeting this condition is less than 95%, the heterogeneity is considered inconclusive. To make this spread easier to interpret, we also report the expected number of our 14 genres whose effects are large enough to fall beyond the SESOI.

## Preregistered Models

### M1: Total Playtime

M1 is the preregistered model for H1: is total playtime across Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam associated with wellbeing? The model is a REWB regression and returns the two coefficients, $\beta_W$ for within-person fluctuations and $\beta_B$ for habitual between-person differences. Each participant receives a random intercept, because people differ in baseline wellbeing, and a random slope for within-person playtime, because the association need not be identical for everyone. Priors are calibrated to the 1–5 outcome scale. The intercept prior is centred on the scale midpoint, and the coefficient priors are weakly informative, leaving effects up to roughly 1 point per hour/day plausible while regularising implausibly large values.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\
\mu_{ij} &= \alpha + \beta_W \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} + \beta_B \text{Time}_{\text{between},j} + u_{0j} + u_{1j} \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} \\
\begin{pmatrix} u_{0j} \\ u_{1j} \end{pmatrix} &\sim \text{Normal}\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right) \\
\alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 3, 2) \\
\beta_W, \beta_B &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 0, 0.5)
\end{aligned}$$

In this and the following model equations, parameters that are not listed take the `brms` default priors: the residual standard deviation $\sigma$ and the standard deviations of the participant-level effects have half-Student-$t$(3, 0, 2.5) priors, and correlation matrices have LKJ(1) priors, which are uniform over the correlation in the two-dimensional case.

### M2: Independent Genre Coefficients

M2 is the preregistered specification for H2. Each of the 14 genres receives its own within-person and between-person coefficient, estimated independently, with a random intercept per participant. Because genre exposures are non-exclusive, they cannot be summed to recover total playtime, and M2 therefore contains no separate total-playtime term. Two departures from the registered specification should be noted: (1) exposures use full attribution rather than primary-genre labels (Deviation D1), and (2) the registered random slopes for all genre terms (28 additional parameters) proved near-singular, so we followed the preregistered contingency plan and retained the random intercept only.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\
\mu_{ij} &= \alpha + \sum_{g=1}^{G}\bigl(\beta_{W,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{within},g,ij} + \beta_{B,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{between},g,j}\bigr) + u_{0j} \\
u_{0j} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau_{\text{pid}}) \\
\alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 3, 2) \\
\beta_{W,g}, \beta_{B,g} &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 0, 0.5)
\end{aligned}$$

## Exploratory Models

The models in this section were not preregistered and are reported as exploratory throughout, together with the daily-timescale refits described at the end of this section.

### M3: Hierarchical Prior

M3 keeps M2's structure but changes how the genre coefficients are estimated, and this change yields a direct answer to H2. Rather than treating the 14 coefficients as unrelated, M3 assumes that they are drawn from a common normal distribution centred at zero and estimates the standard deviation of that distribution, τ~genre~, separately for the within-person and between-person dimensions. τ~genre~ is therefore an estimate of exactly the quantity H2 asks about: how much the genre coefficients differ from one another, expressed in outcome units per hour of play. The shared distribution also produces partial pooling. Estimates for rarely played genres are pulled towards the common centre, whereas genres with ample data retain estimates close to their independent values.

The Half-Normal(0, 0.1) hyperprior on τ is matched to the outcome scale. Genre coefficients are expressed in SWEMWBS points per hour/day, and the smallest effect size of interest is 0.06 on that scale, so a much wider hyperprior would place substantial prior mass on heterogeneity far larger than any effect considered plausible. The sensitivity of the results to halving and doubling this scale is examined in Appendix D. Sampling near τ = 0 is numerically difficult, so we use conservative sampler settings and report divergence counts and R-hat diagnostics for every model alongside the results.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\
\mu_{ij} &= \alpha + \sum_{g=1}^{G}\bigl(\beta_{W,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{within},g,ij} + \beta_{B,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{between},g,j}\bigr) + u_{0j} \\
u_{0j} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau_{\text{pid}}) \\
\beta_{W,g} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau_{\text{within}}) \\
\beta_{B,g} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau_{\text{between}}) \\
\tau_{\text{within}}, \tau_{\text{between}} &\sim \text{Half-Normal}(0, 0.1) \\
\alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 3, 2)
\end{aligned}$$

### M4: Multi-Membership

M4 represents each wave the way panel D of @fig-descriptives displays each day, namely as a total amount of playtime with a genre composition. The model retains total playtime as the predictor, inheriting M1's structure including the overall $\beta_W$ and $\beta_B$, and allows the composition of that playtime to modify the playtime slope. Formally, this is a multi-membership structure, where each wave carries all 14 genre labels and only the weights vary, equal to each genre's share of exposure. Waves with no recorded play receive equal weights of 1/14. As such, a wave consisting mostly of Shooter play is governed mostly by the Shooter slope adjustment, and a wave divided between Adventure and RPG draws on both adjustments in proportion.

Each genre's slope adjustment is drawn from a common distribution, and the standard deviation of that distribution, σ~s~, is this model's answer to H2: it quantifies how much the playtime–wellbeing slope varies with the genres being played. A genre's within-person and between-person adjustments are drawn jointly, with a correlation between them estimated from the data.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\
\mu_{ij} &= \alpha + \beta_W \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} + \beta_B \text{Time}_{\text{between},j} + u_{0j} + u_{1j} \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} \\
&\quad + \sum_{g=1}^{G} w_{g,ij}(s_{W,g} \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} + s_{B,g} \text{Time}_{\text{between},j}) \\
\begin{pmatrix} u_{0j} \\ u_{1j} \end{pmatrix} &\sim \text{Normal}\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\right) \\
\begin{pmatrix} s_{W,g} \\ s_{B,g} \end{pmatrix} &\sim \text{Normal}\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s\right), \quad \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_s^2 & \rho\,\sigma_s \sigma_{s,\text{between}} \\ \rho\,\sigma_s \sigma_{s,\text{between}} & \sigma_{s,\text{between}}^2 \end{pmatrix} \\
\alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 3, 2) \\
\beta_W, \beta_B &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 0, 0.5) \\
\sigma_s, \sigma_{s,\text{between}} &\sim \text{Half-Normal}(0, 0.3) \\
\rho &\sim \text{Uniform}(-1, 1)
\end{aligned}$$

Because this use of multi-membership is unconventional, we validated the specification by parameter recovery before fitting it to real data. Synthetic datasets with known genre-slope heterogeneity were fit with identical model code; every population-level parameter, including σ~s~, was recovered within its 95% credible interval, with no divergent transitions (simulation report in the supplementary materials).

### Daily Timescale

```{r}
#| label: daily-setup

# Exploratory daily-timescale extension. Unregistered; the analysis plan
# (notes/analysis_plan_daily.md, local working docs) fixed the equivalence
# threshold transfer, exposure window, model set, priors, and the coverage
# amendment BEFORE any exposure-outcome model was estimated. Fits are
# produced by R/fit_daily_models.R and cached under models/daily/.

daily_frame_raw <- read_csv(here("data/processed/daily/daily_model_frame.csv"),
                            show_col_types = FALSE)
d_gh_cols <- sort(grep("^gh_", names(daily_frame_raw), value = TRUE))
stopifnot(length(d_gh_cols) == 14, "covered" %in% names(daily_frame_raw))

d_decompose <- function(df) {
  df |>
    group_by(pid) |>
    mutate(
      total_within  = total_hours_today - mean(total_hours_today, na.rm = TRUE),
      total_between = habitual_daily_hours
    ) |>
    ungroup()
}
# Analysed sample: telemetry-covered responses from participants with reliable
# timezone inference, excluding degenerate same-day windows (< 1 h).
daily_frame <- d_decompose(
  daily_frame_raw |>
    filter(covered, !tz_unreliable, window_hours >= 1,
           !is.na(habitual_daily_hours))
)

# Sample and compliance quantities for the prose
d_n_resp_all   <- nrow(daily_frame_raw)
d_n_pid_all    <- n_distinct(daily_frame_raw$pid)
d_n_resp       <- nrow(daily_frame)
d_n_pid        <- n_distinct(daily_frame$pid)

d_median_days  <- median(d_days_per_pid)
d_zero_share   <- mean(daily_frame$total_hours_today == 0)
d_wh_med       <- median(daily_frame$window_hours)
d_n_tz_unrel   <- daily_frame_raw |> filter(tz_unreliable) |> distinct(pid) |> nrow()
d_day1_n       <- sum(daily_frame_raw$day == 1)
d_day30_n      <- sum(daily_frame_raw$day == 30)
d_n_no_tel_pid <- daily_frame_raw |> filter(!has_telemetry) |>
  distinct(pid) |> nrow()
d_n_uncov_resp <- sum(!daily_frame_raw$covered)

# The daily outcome is a 0-100 slider. Its equivalence benchmark is built
# like the registered SESOI: a minimally important difference divided by the
# roughly five hours of daily leisure realistically available.
d_mid_daily  <- 5     # slider points (see text for the convergent anchors)
d_primary    <- d_mid_daily / 5

# Guard the item description the Measures text relies on: the daily slider
# is 0-100, not an 11-point ladder.
stopifnot(
  n_distinct(daily_frame_raw$life_sat[!is.na(daily_frame_raw$life_sat)]) > 11,
  max(daily_frame_raw$life_sat, na.rm = TRUE) > 10
)

# Within-person SDs (used descriptively for the cross-timescale standardised
# comparison in the reading paragraph).
sesoi_d <- readRDS(here("models/daily/sesoi.rds"))
d_within_sd <- function(x, id) {
  d <- tibble(x = x, id = id) |> filter(!is.na(x)) |>
    group_by(id) |> filter(n() >= 2) |> mutate(dev = x - mean(x)) |> ungroup()
  sd(d$dev)
}
stopifnot(
  abs(d_within_sd(daily_frame_raw$life_sat, daily_frame_raw$pid) -
        sesoi_d$s_w_ls) < 1e-6
)

# Correlation between the daily outcome and the momentary valence slider
# (both outcomes; no exposure involved). Quoted in the limitations.
d_ls_av <- daily_frame_raw |> filter(!is.na(life_sat), !is.na(affective_valence))
d_ls_av_r <- cor(d_ls_av$life_sat, d_ls_av$affective_valence)
d_ls_av_rw <- d_ls_av |>
  group_by(pid) |> filter(n() >= 2) |>
  mutate(ls = life_sat - mean(life_sat),
         av = affective_valence - mean(affective_valence)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  summarise(r = cor(ls, av)) |>
  pull(r)

# Positive control 1: self-reported play (past 24 h) vs telemetry in a
# MATCHED 24-hour window; the control keeps the 24 h base precisely because
# the analysis window does not match the self-report item's recall frame.
d_ctrl <- daily_frame_raw |>
  filter(covered24, played24hr %in% c("Yes", "No")) |>
  mutate(self = played24hr == "Yes", tele = total_hours_24h > 0)
d_ctrl_agree <- mean(d_ctrl$self == d_ctrl$tele)
d_ctrl_phi   <- cor(d_ctrl$self, d_ctrl$tele)

# Positive control 2: shooter-gender d in the diary subsample (biweekly
# pipeline exposures; self-contained recode mirroring the Methods recode)
d_intake_g <- read_csv(here("data/clean/survey_intake.csv.gz"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(pid, gender = case_when(
    gender %in% c("Man", "Male")     ~ "Man",
    gender %in% c("Woman", "Female") ~ "Woman",
    gender == "Prefer not to say"    ~ NA_character_,
    is.na(gender)                    ~ NA_character_,
    TRUE                             ~ "Non-binary/Other"
  ))
d_shooter <- read_csv(here("data/processed/genre_wave_long.csv"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(genre == "Shooter") |>
  group_by(pid, wave) |>
  summarise(sh = sum(hours_per_day), .groups = "drop")
d_shooter_pid <- read_csv(here("data/processed/total_playtime.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(pid %in% daily_frame_raw$pid) |>
  distinct(pid) |>
  left_join(d_shooter |> group_by(pid) |> summarise(sh = mean(sh), .groups = "drop"),
            by = "pid") |>
  mutate(sh = replace_na(sh, 0)) |>
  inner_join(d_intake_g, by = "pid") |>
  filter(gender %in% c("Man", "Woman"))
d_sh_m <- d_shooter_pid |> filter(gender == "Man")   |> pull(sh)
d_sh_w <- d_shooter_pid |> filter(gender == "Woman") |> pull(sh)
d_pool_sd   <- sqrt(((length(d_sh_m) - 1) * var(d_sh_m) +
                     (length(d_sh_w) - 1) * var(d_sh_w)) /
                    (length(d_sh_m) + length(d_sh_w) - 2))
d_shooter_d <- (mean(d_sh_m) - mean(d_sh_w)) / d_pool_sd

```

```{r}
#| label: txt-daily-timescale-1
#| include: false

# Inline quantities for the paragraph(s) below, defined once here so the
# prose reads `r name` rather than a formatting call.
txt_d_n_resp_all <- print_num(d_n_resp_all)
txt_d_n_pid_all <- print_num(d_n_pid_all)
txt_d_n_resp <- print_num(d_n_resp)
txt_pct_d_resp_analysed <- round(100 * d_n_resp / d_n_resp_all, 1)
